chunks.title: Provenance & certificates
chunks.heading: What is a certificate of attestation?
chunks.text:
An Attesté certificate is a digital record that attests to an artwork's identity and history. Each certificate carries a cryptographic integrity hash (SHA-256) — if anything in the certificate were altered, the hash would no longer match, so tampering is detectable. Certificate hashes are additionally anchored to the Bitcoin blockchain via OpenTimestamps, which proves the certificate existed at a given point in time without publishing any of its contents.

Unlimited certificates are included from the Collector tier up; artists issue source certificates from their artist plan.

chunks.title: Provenance & certificates
chunks.heading: Verifying a certificate
chunks.text:
Anyone can verify a certificate — no account needed:

- QR code: every certificate has a QR code that opens a public verification view showing the certificate's status and integrity check.

- NFC tag: if the artwork carries an Attesté NFC tag, tapping a phone against it opens the same verification — see NFC tags .

The public view shows only what the certificate holder chose to make verifiable — not your private collection data.

chunks.title: Provenance & certificates

chunks.text:
Talking Provenance (the Curator's Commentary) lets you record spoken provenance — the story of a work in your own voice, guided by the AI Companion. Recordings become permanent, integrity-hashed artefacts attached to the artwork, and travel with it if it is transferred. Recordings are capped at 4 minutes each.

- Recording is available on Premium and Patron collector plans, Artist Professional and Represented plans, and Gallery Professional and Enterprise plans.

- Voice recording asks for its own consent the first time you use it — see the voice-data section of Your account & your data .

chunks.title: NFC tags
chunks.heading: What NFC tags do
chunks.text: A physical NFC tag can be bound to an artwork's certificate of attestation. Once bound, tapping a phone against the tag opens the certificate's verification view — a physical handshake between the artwork and its digital provenance. See Provenance & certificates for what verification shows.

chunks.title: NFC tags
chunks.heading: Scanning a tag
chunks.text:
- Open the Scan NFC screen in the app (or use the scan action on a certificate).

- Hold the top of your phone flat against the tag until it is detected.

- The linked certificate opens automatically.

Tips if a tag isn't reading:

- Make sure NFC is enabled (Android: Settings → Connected devices; iPhone: always on, no setting needed).

- The antenna is at the top edge of most phones — move the phone slowly over the tag.

- Remove thick cases, and avoid metal surfaces directly behind the tag.

- NFC requires the iOS or Android app — the web version can't scan tags.

chunks.title: Art Provenance Glossary
chunks.heading: Provenance
chunks.text:
The documented history of an artwork's ownership, exhibition, and custody — from the moment it was created to the present day.

Provenance is the single biggest factor in an artwork's authenticity and value. A clear, unbroken record tells a buyer that a work is what it claims to be; a thin or broken record raises questions that can be expensive to answer later.

chunks.title: Art Provenance Glossary
chunks.heading: Certificate of Authenticity
chunks.text:
A document attesting that an artwork is genuine and recording its key facts — artist, title, medium, dimensions, and year.

A certificate is only as trustworthy as the person who issued it and the ease with which it can be checked. A certificate that cannot be independently verified carries little weight; one backed by the artist and a tamper-evident record carries a great deal.

chunks.title: Art Provenance Glossary
chunks.heading: Source Certificate
chunks.text:
A certificate issued by the artist directly from their studio, confirming authorship at the point of origin.

Because it comes from the source rather than being reconstructed years later, a source certificate is the gold-standard provenance record — the strongest possible starting point for the chain a collector carries forward.

chunks.title: Art Provenance Glossary
chunks.heading: Attestation
chunks.text:
A formal, recorded statement that something is true — here, a signed assertion about an artwork's authorship, ownership, or history.

The word gives Attesté its name. An attestation is only meaningful if it can be checked, which is why a credible attestation pairs a clear statement with the means to verify it.

chunks.title: Art Provenance Glossary
chunks.heading: Chain of Custody
chunks.text:
The unbroken, ordered record of everyone who has owned or held an artwork over time.

Each ownership change is a link in the chain. Gaps weaken provenance, because an undocumented period is a period in which a work's identity cannot be vouched for. A complete chain — where every transfer is recorded and verifiable — is what separates a confident sale from a cautious one.

chunks.title: Art Provenance Glossary
chunks.heading: SHA-256 Integrity Hash
chunks.text:
A unique cryptographic fingerprint calculated from a certificate's exact contents.

Change a single character of the record and the fingerprint changes completely. That property makes the hash a tamper detector: anyone can recompute it and confirm the certificate has not been altered since it was issued.

chunks.title: Art Provenance Glossary
chunks.heading: Bitcoin Anchoring
chunks.text:
Recording a certificate's fingerprint onto the Bitcoin blockchain — via the open OpenTimestamps standard — so its existence at a given moment can be proven independently.

This is what makes a record outlast its issuer. Even if the original platform disappears, the holder of a certificate can prove it existed at the timestamped moment using only the proof file and any Bitcoin node. Independent verifiability, not platform trust, is the point.

chunks.title: Art Provenance Glossary
chunks.heading: Tamper-Evident Record
chunks.text:
A record built so that any alteration is immediately detectable.

Tamper-evident is a stronger, more honest claim than "tamper-proof." It does not pretend a record can never be changed — it guarantees that changes cannot be hidden. For provenance, that is exactly what matters: not that history is frozen, but that any rewriting of it is visible.

chunks.title: Art Provenance Glossary
chunks.heading: Talking Provenance
chunks.text:
Spoken commentary about an artwork — by the artist, the gallery, or the collector — captured as a permanent recording that travels with the work.

For five centuries the knowledge behind a work lived in private letters and was lost when galleries closed and owners passed on. Talking Provenance captures it instead: a hash-chained recording, attributed to its speaker, that becomes part of the chain of custody. It preserves the context that paper records cannot.

chunks.title: Art Provenance Glossary
chunks.heading: First Witness
chunks.text:
The very first record in an artwork’s provenance chain — made by the artist, in their own voice, at the moment of creation.

Every other approach reconstructs provenance backwards, years later, from whatever paper survived. First Witness records it forward: when an artist registers a new work, they record its story themselves, and that account is sealed with a SHA-256 fingerprint and Bitcoin-anchored as the origin every later link builds on. Recorded at the source and never backfillable, it is the strongest possible starting point a work can have — and no record made after the fact can replace it.

chunks.title: Art Provenance Glossary
chunks.heading: Catalogue Raisonné
chunks.text:
A comprehensive, scholarly listing of all known works by an artist, used as the reference for authenticity.

Inclusion in the catalogue raisonné is one of the strongest external signals of a work's legitimacy; absence from one can be a red flag worth investigating before a purchase.

chunks.title: Art Provenance Glossary
chunks.heading: Condition Report
chunks.text:
A detailed account of an artwork's physical state at a point in time — damage, restoration, wear, and any conservation work.

Condition is part of provenance. A documented condition history affects value and insurability, and protects both buyer and seller by recording exactly how a work looked when it changed hands.

chunks.title: Art Provenance Glossary
chunks.heading: Estimated Value
chunks.text:
An informed estimate of what an artwork is worth.

Attesté treats documented evidence as authoritative — an invoice, a professional valuation, a formal revaluation — in that order. Any experimental AI estimate is kept clearly separate and never counted in a collection's value. When it comes to worth, the receipt is king.

chunks.title: Attesté
chunks.heading: Frequently Asked
chunks.text:
Straight answers on cost, privacy, provenance, and how the AI works.

What is Attesté?
Attesté is an AI-powered art collection management platform. It helps collectors catalogue their art, verify provenance with SHA-256 cryptographic certificates, discover new galleries and artists via GPS-gated trails, and document collection history across generations.

How much does Attesté cost?
Attesté has a free Explorer tier (25 artworks, 5 AI analyses/month). Paid collector tiers start at $9.99/month (Collector — 200 artworks, full AI Sommelier) and $19.99/month (Premium — unlimited, Legacy Vault), with 17% savings on annual plans. Artist plans start at $14.99/month (Studio, 14-day free trial). Gallery plans are monthly subscriptions sold via the web: Boutique $64.99/mo, Professional $158.99/mo, Enterprise $259.00/mo.

Is my art collection data private?
Yes. By default every collection is private. Public profiles require an explicit opt-in. Data is hosted in Firebase's Johannesburg data centre (africa-south1), so personal data stays in Africa by default. Attesté is POPIA and GDPR aware.

How does AI Art Identification work?
You photograph an artwork with the Attesté app. Google's latest Gemini vision models analyse the image and return likely artist, medium, period and similar works, with an explicit confidence score. Low-confidence guesses are flagged for human verification.

What is an Attesté Certificate?
A SHA-256 cryptographically-secured provenance certificate. It includes the owner, acquisition date and source, a photograph fingerprint, condition and valuation history, and the chain of custody. The hash is published to an immutable log so tampering is detectable.

Does Attesté authenticate whether an artwork is real?
No. Attesté generates a tamper-proof record of what the owner reported. Authentication is a gallery, auction house or expert's job. You can upload professional authentication documents and attach them to the certificate.

Can Attesté help me document an inherited art collection?
Yes. Attesté's AI Art Scout is especially useful for inheritors: photograph each piece and the app identifies likely artist, medium and period. Upgrade to Premium to unlock the Legacy Vault for preserving stories, artist interviews, and acquisition context across generations.

How do galleries use Attesté?
Galleries join on a monthly subscription sold via the web — Boutique ($64.99/mo), Professional ($158.99/mo), or Enterprise ($259.00/mo). They get inventory and exhibition tools, an aggregate collector analytics dashboard, Talking Provenance Curator's Commentary (Professional+), AI-generated exhibition posts, a daily Pulse briefing, the Almanac AI concierge, and a measurable collector pipeline. Analytics are aggregate-only — individual collector data is never shared with galleries.

Where is Attesté available?
The Attesté app works worldwide. POPIA compliance (South Africa) is complete; GDPR compliance (EU) is in progress; US and UK markets are supported. Payment methods vary by region. Contact info@atteste.art for your specific market.

Who built Attesté?
Attesté is built by Yield SPM (Pty) Ltd, founded by Karel Kraai in Bloemfontein, South Africa. Company registration: 2024/185151/07. The same team also operates Practacular, an AI practice management platform for accountants.
